statement.p: (b) What does your answer to part (a) tell you about \int_C\vec F\cdot d\vec r where C is the circle (x-20)^2+(y-5)^2=1 in the xy-plane, oriented clockwise?
(c) If C is any closed curve, what can you say about \int_C \vec F\cdot d\vec r?

(d) Now let C be the half circle (x-20)^2+(y-5)^2=1 in the xy-plane with y > 5, traversed from (21, 5) to (19, 5). Find \int_C \vec F\cdot d\vec r by using your result from (c) and considering C plus the line segment connecting the endpoints of C.

static.solution:
(a) Let \vec F=\left(6z+6x^{2}\right)\,\mathit{\vec i}+\left(5y+6z+6\sin\mathopen{}\left(y^{2}\right)\right)\,\mathit{\vec j}+\left(6x+6y+5e^{z^{2}}\right)\,\mathit{\vec k}. Then \mbox{curl }\vec F = \left| \begin{array}{ccc} \vec i \amp \vec j \amp \vec k\\ \frac{\partial}{\partial x} \amp \frac{\partial}{\partial y} \amp \frac{\partial}{\partial z} \\ 6(z + x^{2}) \amp 5 y + 6(z + sin(y^{2})) \ \amp 6 x + 6 y + 5 e^{z^{2}} \end{array} \right| = \vec 0.
(b) Since C is a closed curve, \int_C\vec F\cdot d\vec r=0 by Stokes' Theorem.
(c) The line integral is 0 for any closed curve C in 3-space.
(d) Let C_1 be the line segment from (19, 5) to (21, 5). Then, by (c), we know \int_{C + C_1}\vec F\cdot d\vec r = \int_{C}\vec F\cdot d\vec r + \int_{C_1}\vec F\cdot d\vec r = 0. Thus \int_{C}\vec F\cdot d\vec r = -\int_{C_1}\vec F\cdot d\vec r. On C_1, we have 19\le x\le 21, y = 5 and z = 0, so \int_{C_1}\vec F\cdot d\vec r = \int_{19}^{21}\,0 + 6 x^{2}\,dx = 2\,x^{3}\bigg|_{19}^{21} = 4804. Thus \int_{C}\vec F\cdot d\vec r = -4804.
